{"evidence":[{"sentence_id":0,"text":"Zamia is a genus of cycad of the family Zamiaceae, native to Mexico, the West Indies, and Central and South America as far south as Bolivia.","title":"Zamia"},{"sentence_id":1,"text":" The range of one species (\"Z. integrifolia\", extends into the contiguous United States, i.e. Georgia and Florida.","title":"Zamia"},{"sentence_id":0,"text":"Delphinium staphisagria is a species of \"Delphinium\", or larkspur, of the family Ranunculaceae.","title":"Delphinium staphisagria"},{"sentence_id":1,"text":" This plant is also known as Lice-Bane or Stavesacre.","title":"Delphinium staphisagria"},{"sentence_id":2,"text":" It is described botanically as a stoutly-stemmed, hairy biennial with large palmate leaves up to 6 inches (15 cm) across.","title":"Delphinium staphisagria"},{"sentence_id":3,"text":" The flowers are mauve-blue to blue, short-spurred, and up to 1 inch (2.5 cm) across, occurring in racemes.","title":"Delphinium staphisagria"},{"sentence_id":4,"text":" The plant grows to a height of 4–5 feet.","title":"Delphinium staphisagria"},{"sentence_id":5,"text":" It grows throughout the Mediterranean.","title":"Delphinium staphisagria"},{"sentence_id":6,"text":" The dark-colored, wrinkled seeds of \"D. staphisagria\" are characteristically quite large (~5x6 mm), and it is likely that the species name, which translates to \"wild raisin\" (classical Greek: σταφὶς ἀγρία) is based on their appearance.","title":"Delphinium staphisagria"},{"sentence_id":7,"text":" This name-derivation seems to have been arrived at independently by a modern horticulturalist, David Bassett, who also gives a detailed account of his experiences in growing this species.","title":"Delphinium staphisagria"},{"sentence_id":8,"text":" All parts of this plant are highly toxic and should not be ingested in any quantity.","title":"Delphinium staphisagria"}],"peer_messages":[],"previous_answer":null,"question":"Which plant grows further North, Zamia or Vallea?"}
